sections.heading: Dialogue I, Knot xi (printed pp. 96–101)
rows: [p. 96] [Margin: Nodus XI. Tubum opticum in summo esse.] Asphal. Ergo ad tubos coelispices nos remittis, ut inde secreta harum rerum indicia hauriamus, ex quibus ulterius in hac scientia proficere liceat.

[p. 96] [Margin: Knot XI. That the optic tube is at the highest [in summo].] Asphal. Therefore you send us back to the heaven-viewing tubes [tubos coelispices], that thence we may draw [hauriamus] the secret indications [indicia] of these things, from which it may be permitted to advance [proficere] further in this science.

Ereu. Heu! quam vereor ne etiam illi nos destituant? suspicor enim quod in pluribus etiam in iis usu venisse, ut nemo ad primos artifices pertingat. Et sicut Homerum vel Archimedem nulla aetas secundum vidit, ita neque parem Galilaeano alium tubum unquam videamus, certe nihilo meliorem.

Ereu. Alas! how I fear lest those too forsake us? For I suspect that [quod] [it has] happened [usu venisse] in many [things], also in these, that no one reaches to the first artificers. And just as no age has seen a second Homer or Archimedes, so neither may we ever see another tube equal to the Galilean, certainly none [nihilo] better.
Asphal. Quid ais, Ereuni? Tu solus nescis novam horum condendorum scientiam ab aliquot annis lucem vidisse a magni nominis parente.

Asphal. What do you say, Ereunius? Are you alone ignorant [that] a new science of making [condendorum] these [tubes] has seen the light some years since [ab aliquot annis] from a parent of great name?

[Margin: Liber ingeniosissimus Renati de Cartes.] Ereu. Non sum ignarus; sed hoc ipsum primo me exanimat, quod tot annis non respondit eventus auspicio. Neque librum ipsum neglexi et divinum viri ingenium quam maxime [p. 97] sum demiratus, tam graviter multa et abditissima quidem promit, tam dilucide obscurissima quaeque explanat, experimentis confirmat, et subtilissimis rationibus acutissime pleraque concludit; et est uno verbo Philosophiae spes altera. Sed non omnia ab uno aliquo sperari possunt sine naturae calumnia et ipsius a quo pendet iniuria.

[Margin: The most ingenious book of René Descartes.] Ereu. I am not ignorant; but this very thing first [primo] disheartens [exanimat] me, that in so many years the outcome [eventus] has not answered to the auspice [auspicio]. Nor have I neglected the book itself, and I have [p. 97] marvelled [demiratus] as greatly as possible at the divine wit [ingenium] of the man: so weightily does he bring forth [promit] many and indeed most hidden things, so lucidly does he explain all the most obscure things, confirms [them] by experiments [experimentis], and with most subtle reasons [rationibus] most acutely concludes most [things]; and he is, in one word, the second hope [spes altera] of Philosophy. But not all things can be hoped for from some one [man] without cavil [calumnia] against nature and injury to Him on whom it depends [ipsius a quo pendet].

Asphal. Quid est itaque quod tibi in illo displicet? quo minus hoc ei votum successurum putes? Magna enim, nisi fallor, pollicetur, et nisi artificis nos deficiat manus, in Coelis tam distincta, et tam exigua se proditurum, quam ea sunt quibus assuevimus in terris.

Asphal. What is it, therefore, that displeases you in him? for which [reason] the less [quo minus] you think this wish [votum] will succeed for him? For he promises great things, unless I am mistaken, and [that], unless the hand of the artificer fail us, he will bring forth [proditurum] in the Heavens [things] as distinct and as small as are those to which we have grown accustomed on earth.

Ereu. Huiusmodi dicta ad excitandos artificum labores iactari interdum expedit, neque enim credam ipsum de hoc ambegisse, sed certo scivisse defuturas artificum manus. Quid enim putas futurum, cum circulus, in ea magnitudine cuius usum habemus, a linea recta, nullo sensu distingui poterit? Et tantumdem est de hyperbola qua ille utitur: quoad hoc enim parva est differentia. Quid cum tubus tam longus est evasurus, ut visui nostro coeant eius latera? Praeterea si homo in luna foret spectandus, nonne hoc necessarium est ut per eos radios spectetur qui ab ipso de luna affluunt? Confer horum vigorem, cum ad nos perveniunt, vigori pili in ti-[p. 98]bia pulicis, quem tamen, nisi multiplicato lumine per auxilium perspicilli explicatorii videre nequimus, et cogita quid sperandum? Corroborare enim lumen ab homine in luna existente nulla ars valebit. Adde quod nisi sic hominem videamus ut praeterea nihil quod eum obfuscare possit, frustra eum credimus spectabilem, ingentia enim spectabilia minorum aspectum tollunt. Quem autem modum suspicari possumus prohibendi caeteris quae in luna hominem comitantur, longe illo maiora tubi et vitrorum aditu? Et haec quidem tam parva videri non posse persuadent.

Ereu. It is expedient [expedit] that sayings of this kind be thrown out [iactari] sometimes to stir up the labours of artificers; for neither would I believe that he himself wavered [ambegisse] about this, but [that he] knew for certain that the hands of artificers would be lacking. For what do you think will be [futurum], when a circle, in that magnitude of which we have use, will be able to be distinguished by no sense from a straight line? And it is just the same [tantumdem] concerning the hyperbola which he uses: for as regards [quoad] this the difference is small. What [of it] when the tube is going to turn out [evasurus] so long that its sides come together [coeant] to our sight? Moreover, if a man in the moon were to be looked at, is it not necessary that he be looked at through those rays which flow [affluunt] from him himself from the moon? Compare the vigour [vigorem] of these, when they arrive to us, with the vigour of a hair on the [p. 98] leg [tibia] of a flea, which nevertheless we cannot see unless the light be multiplied by the help of an unfolding spy-glass [perspicilli explicatorii], and consider what is to be hoped? For no art will avail to strengthen [corroborare] the light from a man existing in the moon. Add that unless we see the man so that besides [him there is] nothing which could obscure him, in vain do we believe him visible [spectabilem]; for huge visible things take away the sight [aspectum] of smaller ones. But what mode can we suspect of keeping [prohibendi] the other things which accompany the man in the moon, far greater than he, from access [aditu] to the tube and the glasses? And these [considerations] indeed persuade [us] that things so small cannot be seen.

Sed quod me terret, et ad hoc adigit, ut non multum profecturam hanc artem credam, est quod mihi certo persuadeam neque res videri maiores, nisi et iam propiores appareant, neque propiores nisi maioribus angulis et conis occupent oculum; anguli autem visorii eadem vi decrescunt qua approximatio obiecti augetur: Unde necessum est ad medium quoddam excellentiae cito perveniri. Tantumdem est quod ex vitris contrariis concavo scilicet et convexo resultat tubus, quorum et hanc proprietatum oppositionem advertimus, convexa vitra, quo maioris sphaerae portiones sunt, eo confusiorem exhibere visi speciem: concava e diverso, quo minorum sphaerarum scaphia sunt, eo distinctiorem [p. 99] eandem pingere: ut idem ipsum ex his decerpas, proportione comparari debere partes tubi, quae magnam latitudinem habere non possit. Timori quoque est mihi Galilaeus qui Catoptrica Archimedis legit cum summo stupore, et addit hoc elogium, omnia miracula quae de Archimede narrantur, per eam lectionem sibi credibilia facta esse: hic ergo tam curiosus coeli spectator, tam avidus novorum instrumentorum, cessaret si aliud suo longe melius sperare posset?

But what frightens me, and drives [adigit] [me] to this, that I believe this art will not advance much, is that I persuade myself for certain [that] neither are things seen greater unless they also [et iam] appear nearer, nor nearer unless they occupy the eye with greater angles and cones; but the visual [visorii] angles decrease with the same force with which the approximation of the object is increased: whence it is necessary [necessum] that one arrive quickly at a certain middle [point] [medium] of excellence. It is just the same [tantumdem] [with the fact] that the tube results from contrary glasses, namely concave and convex, of which we advert [advertimus] also this opposition of properties: [that] convex glasses, the greater the sphere of which they are portions, the more confused the appearance [speciem] of the thing seen they exhibit; concave [ones], on the contrary [e diverso], the smaller the spheres of which they are bowls [scaphia], the more distinct they [p. 99] paint the same: so that you may pluck [decerpas] this very same thing from these, that the parts of the tube, which [tube] cannot have a great breadth [latitudinem], must be compared by proportion. Galileo also is [a cause] of fear to me [timori … est mihi], who read the Catoptrics of Archimedes with the highest astonishment [stupore], and adds this eulogy: [that] all the miracles which are narrated of Archimedes have been made credible to him through that reading. Would this man, then, so curious a spectator of heaven, so avid of new instruments, cease [cessaret] if he could hope for another [tube] far better than his own?
Asphal. His satis assentior, sed quid ad haec facit Galilaeum Catoptrica Archimedis legisse?
Asphal. I assent sufficiently to these things; but what does it make [facit] for these [matters] that Galileo read the Catoptrics of Archimedes?

[Margin: Catoptrica esse fundamentum Dioptricorum.] Ereu. Quianam Catoptrica fundamenta sunt Dioptricorum; ut expertus sum, cum aliquando desiderio promovendae caelestium cognitionis me applicarem considerandae compositioni tubi optici, et inveni vitri convexi cum speculo concavo, vitri vero concavi cum speculo convexo cognationem esse maximam, et observatis quibusdam regulis, fere omnia eadem contingere: Et si non oculi et otium me defecisset, nescio quid sperare fuisset datum. Sed dum a fundamentis rem excutio et Catoptrica (satis indiligenter ut mihi videtur tractata) penitus dispicere volo, praesertim vero leges luminis cum circuli legibus, stupenda illa in speculo concavo patrantes, et postmodum [p. 100] refractionis naturam investigo, nimio lumine caligaverunt oculi, et monuerunt quod satis est etiam in scientiis observandum.

[Margin: That Catoptrics is the foundation of Dioptrics.] Ereu. Because [quianam] Catoptrics are the foundations of Dioptrics; as I have experienced, when at some time, from desire of promoting the knowledge [cognitionis] of celestial [things], I applied myself to considering the composition of the optic tube, and found that the kinship [cognationem] of the convex glass with the concave mirror, and of the concave glass with the convex mirror, is very great, and [that], certain rules being observed, almost all the same things happen: and if eyes and leisure had not failed me, I know not what it would have been granted [datum] [me] to hope. But while I shake out [excutio] the matter from the foundations, and wish to look thoroughly through [dispicere] the Catoptrics (treated rather [satis] carelessly, as it seems to me), but especially the laws of light, [which,] together with the laws of the circle, accomplish [patrantes] those stupendous [effects] in the concave mirror, and afterwards [p. 100] investigate the nature of refraction, my eyes grew dim [caligaverunt] from too much light, and warned [me] that what is enough [quod satis est] is to be observed also in the sciences.
Andab. Satis ergo de his. Tantum memineris corpora caelestia siquidem ex nostris elementis composita sint, propediem ruitura.
Andab. Enough, then, of these things. Only remember [that] the celestial bodies, if indeed [siquidem] they are composed of our elements, will very soon [propediem] fall in ruin [ruitura].

Ereu. Ignosce, Andabata, vere enim neglexeram, sed oblivione et ipsarum rerum Maeandris abstractus: nunc ergo ad te redeo, et hoc primo peto. Magnetem et totum magneticorum genus, Electrum quoque cum tota Electricorum familia num putes ex elementis nostris esse concreta?

Ereu. Forgive [me], Andabata, for truly I had neglected [it], but [I was] drawn away by forgetfulness and by the Meanders of the things themselves: now therefore I return to you, and this I ask first. The Magnet and the whole kind of magnetic [things], Amber [Electrum] also with the whole family of Electric [things]: do you think [num putes] [that they] are concreted [concreta] out of our elements?
[Margin: Astra cur non cadant in terram.] Andab. Quidni sentiam?
[Margin: Why the Stars do not fall onto the earth.] Andab. Why should I not think [so]?
Ereu. Cur itaque in terram non ruunt quae ab iis attrahuntur, quod facerent, si haec abessent?
Ereu. Why therefore do the things which are attracted by them not rush down [ruunt] onto the earth, which they would do if these were absent?
Andab. Quia fortius attrahuntur ab Electro vel magnete quam a terra.
Andab. Because they are attracted more strongly by the Amber or the magnet than by the earth.
Ereu. Ergo et quae a luna vel alio Astro elevantur, si fortius ab eo attrahantur, quam a terra, in illud magis recident quam in terram.

Ereu. Therefore also the things which are raised [elevantur] from the moon or another Star, if they are attracted more strongly by it than by the earth, will fall back [recident] into it rather than onto the earth.
Andab. Recte: sed quid ipsum Astrum trahet, ne totum cum omnibus sibi adhaerentibus concidat? Sicut haec quae nominas Electrica et magnetica facere cottidie experimenta capimus.

Andab. Rightly: but what will draw the Star itself, lest it fall down [concidat] whole with all the things adhering to it? Just as we daily take experiments [experimenta capimus] [that] these [things] which you name Electric and magnetic do [facere].

[p. 101] Ereu. Ast ego contra interrogo quid deorsum ea trahet? si enim Aristotelis discipulus es, nosti gravia et levia non a se, sed a generante moveri, quale autem inter astra generans sis positurus quae ea ad terram moveat, nondum capio. Non si tellurem quanta quanta est, magnetem efficias, credam te vim ipsius usque ad octavum coelum expansurum.

[p. 101] Ereu. But I on the contrary ask: what will draw them downward? for if you are a disciple of Aristotle, you know [that] heavy and light [things] are moved not by themselves but by the generator [a generante]; but what sort of generator you are going to place among the stars, which [quae] would move them to the earth, I do not yet grasp. Not if you should make the earth [tellurem], however great it is [quanta quanta est], a magnet, would I believe that you would expand its force as far as the eighth heaven.
Andab. Fateor me doctrinam hanc de generante nunquam intellexisse, neque multum probare, et in hac parte reddere Aristoteli quod ipse Platoni.
Andab. I confess that I have never understood this doctrine concerning the generator, nor much approve [it], and in this part [I] render to Aristotle what he himself [rendered] to Plato.

[Margin: Quid sit generans quod movet gravia et levia.] Ereu. Neque ego, Andabata, libens me immittam gravium et levium discussioni, rei satis perplexae, tum quia nox iam gravior imminet, tum quia aureo illi libello quem saepius ante commemini, praeripere vivacitatem et quasi aciem obtundere, scelus foret. Hoc tamen in Lycaei gratiam dictum esto. Generans apud Aristotelem non unum aliquod signatum agens, sed ipsam seriem causarum quae universaliter ad generationem concurrunt, appellari, quae quia nusquam deest, in media luce palpitant, qui nescio quae singularia agentia venantur.

[Margin: What the generator is which moves heavy and light [things].] Ereu. Nor would I, Andabata, willingly launch myself [me immittam] into the discussion of heavy and light [things], a matter quite [satis] perplexed, both because night, now heavier, is impending, and because it would be a crime to snatch beforehand [praeripere] the liveliness [vivacitatem] from that golden little book which I have mentioned [commemini] rather often before, and as it were to blunt its edge [aciem]. Let this, however, be said for the sake [in gratiam] of the Lyceum: [that] the generator in Aristotle is called [appellari] not some one signate [signatum] agent, but the very series of causes which concur universally to generation; which [series], because it is nowhere lacking, they grope [palpitant] in the midst of the light who hunt for I know not what singular agents.

terms: telescope; coelispex is a rare coinage ('heaven-looker')
Cf. tubus astrisequus (FM2) and tubus opticus (margin): White varies the name of the telescope.
at its peak / perfection; at the top (location)
The nodus shows the meaning: the telescope has already reached the limit of its perfection (Galileo's tube will not be surpassed). Resolves FM2 uncertain reading (7).
Liber ingeniosissimus Renati de Cartes / spes altera
most ingenious book of René Descartes / second hope
Descartes's Dioptrique (1637, with the Discours); 'spes altera' echoes Virgil, Aen. XII.168 (Ascanius, 'magnae spes altera Romae')
Descartes claimed that with perfected hyperbolic lenses one might see objects on the moon as small as animals; White doubts it.
or: of [Descartes] himself, on whom [the hope] depends
Most naturally God, on whom nature depends; ambiguity kept.
as printed; probably for ambigisse (ambigo) or misprint
Descartes's Dioptrique, Discours VIII–X, prescribes hyperbolic and elliptical lens surfaces to avoid spherical aberration.
explicare = unfold, spread out (enlarge); the flea's leg is the stock early-microscope object.
Euclidean–Alhazenian optics: apparent size by visual angle of the visual cone.
hollow vessel; concave segment of a sphere
Greek σκάφιον; also the name of a concave sundial.
Pseudo-Euclidean and (lost) Archimedean catoptrics; Descartes's Dioptrique.
is [a cause] of fear to me
Galileo's praise of Archimedes is not identified exactly here (cf. Galileo's admiration of Archimedes in the Saggiatore and Discorsi).
White's observation of the optical equivalence of a convex lens and a concave mirror.
Play on 'nimio lumine': his eyes, dazzled by too much light, teach measure in the sciences.
amber; bodies that attract like amber
Of mixts made out of the elements.
generator / be moved by the generator
the begetter; per accidens mover of heavy and light bodies
Aristotle, Phys. VIII.4, 255b: heavy and light things are moved by that which generated them (or by the remover of an obstacle).
Cf. signabilis / designabilis in the glossary.
render to Aristotle what he himself [rendered] to Plato
Allusion to 'amicus Plato, sed magis amica veritas'.
Digby's treatise (Two Treatises, 1644, then in preparation)
Cf. D1-N08 'libellus de immortalitate animae'; Digby treats gravity there.
in gratiam = for the sake / in favour of (cf. glossary gratia).
notes: Unit: Dialogue I, Knot xi, complete in one part. PDF pp. 107–112 = printed pp. 96–101, from 'Asphal. Ergo ad tubos coelispices' (p. 96) to '…qui nescio quae singularia agentia venantur.' (p. 101). Knot xii begins on p. 101 (PDF 112) at 'Asphal. Tam leviter itaque nobis praeripis notionem telluris', margin 'Nodus XII. Tellurem non esse magnetem'. Offset +11 holds (p. 101 = PDF 112).

Title: the margin reads 'Tubum opticum in summo esse'; the FM2 table reads 'Tubum astrisequum in summo esse'. The content (the telescope cannot be much improved beyond Galileo's) shows 'in summo' = at its height/perfection.

Readings: (a) p. 97 'ambegisse' as printed (for ambigisse?). (b) p. 98 'credimus' from blotted 'cre.limus'. (c) p. 98 'proprietatum' (gen. pl.) as printed. (d) p. 99 'ex his' from printed 'ea his' (misprint corrected; {?ex}). (e) p. 99 'quae magnam latitudinem habere non possit': singular, referred to 'tubus' (or misprint for possint, referring to partes). (f) p. 99 'defecisset' singular with two subjects, as printed. (g) p. 101 'Lycaei' from printed 'lyceai'/'lycæi' {?Lycaei}. (h) p. 101 'palpitant' as printed (sense = palpant, grope). (i) p. 100 'cottidie' as printed.

Sense: p. 98 'anguli autem visorii eadem vi decrescunt qua approximatio obiecti augetur' is rendered literally; the argument (magnification has a natural limit, an 'optimum middle of excellence') is White's, not modern optics. p. 100 Andabata's 'Sicut haec … facere cottidie experimenta capimus' is elliptical: perhaps 'as we daily find by experiment that electric and magnetic bodies do [i.e., fall]'.

Verification pass: 4 corrections — (1) word order of 'in pluribus etiam in iis usu venisse'; (2) 'quo minus … putes' re-rendered 'for which [reason] the less'; (3) 'facta esse' in indirect speech rendered 'have been made' (not 'had been'); (4) 'cessaret si … posset' rendered as present unreal 'would … cease … if he could'.
